content_voiceover: This table is high yield for boards, comparing the three classic cold-induced conditions: paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria, cold agglutinin disease, and cryoglobulinemia. Age is a great discriminator, PCH favors children, while cold agglutinin disease and cryoglobulinemia favor older adults. Associated conditions differ too. PCH links to syphilis or post-viral infection, cold agglutinin disease links to lymphoma or other lymphoproliferative disorders, or infections like mycoplasma and mono, and cryoglobulinemia links to hepatitis C, autoimmune disease, and lymphoproliferative disorders. Both PCH and cold agglutinin disease cause true hemolysis with a DAT that's C3 positive but IgG negative, while cryoglobulinemia causes no hemolysis at all, it precipitates instead. The antibody itself is the mechanistic key. PCH uses a cold-reacting IgG biphasic antibody against the P antigen. Cold agglutinin disease uses a cold-reacting IgM against I or i antigen that agglutinates and fixes complement. Cryoglobulinemia isn't really an anti-RBC antibody at all, it's a mixture of antibodies and complement that precipitates out of serum when chilled to four degrees.
keypoints: PCH: children, post-viral or syphilis, IgG biphasic anti-P, causes hemolysis
Cold agglutinin disease: adults, lymphoma or infection, IgM anti-I/i, causes hemolysis
Cryoglobulinemia: adults, HCV or autoimmune disease, NO hemolysis -- precipitates in cold instead
PCH and cold agglutinin disease both show DAT C3-positive, IgG-negative
keypoint_voiceover: PCH occurs in children after viral infection or syphilis, driven by a biphasic IgG against the P antigen, and causes hemolysis. Cold agglutinin disease occurs in adults with lymphoma or infection, driven by IgM against I or i antigen, and also causes hemolysis. Both have a DAT that's C3 positive, IgG negative. Cryoglobulinemia, by contrast, causes no hemolysis, it's antibody and complement precipitating in the cold, linked to hepatitis C and autoimmune disease.
